Grace joined the lab in August 2022, the first official member of the dela Cerna lab when it opened at Georgia Southern, as an undergraduate researcher. Averitt Award for Contributions and Achievements in Research. She is currently a Research Assistant in the lab and plans to pursue a PhD in Biomedical Sciences in the near future.

title: Major Lab News
text:
2026 Jan 25
    
    
      New Year, New Webiste
      This is our first major revamp of our lab website. We have migrated some major news, but it has been a busy past three years and the lab has grown! Several students have gotten their own research grants and scholarships, both internal and external. Several have graduated and are now off to bigger adventures. We will try to keep this new online home for our lab updated with major news as they happen.
      
        General
      
    
  

  
    2025 Dec 16
    
    
      Mark represents Savannah at the GMRS
      The Georgia Magnetic Resonance Symposium 2025 was held at the Georgia Institute of Technology. Mark gave a talk on the applications of solution NMR spectroscopy to the lab's efforts of finding inhibitors of PRL3. He also shared preliminary insights from the SynZyme CURE, developed with Dr. Shainaz Landge.
      
        Invited Talk
      
    
  

  
    2025 Dec 06
    
    
      Chase's work from Bellarmine available online.
      Long time coming, but it's finally out. Chase Yost's work with our lab and Dr. Savita Chaurasia from Bellarmine University entitled, Eriodictyon californicum Extract Inhibits Therapeutically Relevant Protein Tyrosine Phosphatase 1B is now published at the Research Journal of Pharmacy and Technology. This is Chase's first first author paper. Congratulations Chase!
      
        Student
        Publication
      
    
  

  
    2025 Dec 05
    
    
      Year 2 Olympics: Mark goes down.
      Mark is not able to defend his championship as Alicia takes the Ultimate Champion Trophy in this year's version of the Lab Olympics. Grace hosted the lab party at her new home (thank you, Grace!). This year, we have two major awards: the 2025 Lab Member of the Year Award goes to Ruby Pitts, who has already graduated and is currently a research assistant at Vanderbilt, and the inaugural 2025 Rising Star Award to Hannah Scroggins, who has been an outstanding first-year member! We expect great things from both of them!
      
      
        Lab Olympics
        Student
      
    
  

  
    2025 Oct 17
    
    
      Mark gives a talk at DLSU and survives (Ateneo joke)
      Mark gave an invited talk virtually at the Department of Chemistry, De La Salle University in the Philippines. Looking forward to collaborations with DLSU faculty in the future!
      
        Invited Talk
      
    
  

  
    2025 Aug 20
    
    
      Another NIH Grant funded!
      We're thrilled to have our NIH S15 application funded. This will allow us to purchase two high-speed centrifuges that not only supports our current work (makes our purification pipeline more efficient) but also enables additional research. This is so exciting!
      
      
        Grant
      
    
  

  
    2025 Aug 15
    
    
      COSM Excellence Awardee in the house!
      Mark was recognized by a COSM Excellence in Research Award for 2025!
      
      
        Award
      
    
  

  
    2025 Apr 25
    
    
      Grace bestowed with highest award for GS grad students!
      This year, Grace's excellent work so far was acknowledged and recognized by an Averitt Award for Excellence in Research. The Averitt Awards are the highest honors bestowed upon graduate students at Georgia Southern's Graduate School. Congratulations!!
      
      
        Award
      
    
  

  
    2025 Feb 15
    
    
      Our first press release!
      Our work on PRL3 and development of cancer metastasis was featured in Grice Connect, Statesboro-Bulloch County news.
      
      
        General
      
    
  

  
    2024 Dec 13
    
    
      The inaugural lab olympics: Mark DOMINATES
      The lab ended the year with our annual State of the Lab Address by Mark. It also featured our inaugural Lab Olympics. There were a total of nine different events. This year, Mark (winning 3 of the 9 events) was awarded the ultimate champion award. Needless to say, there is a huge target on his back for next year -- the lab is coming for you!! We thank MS student Grace for organizing the olympics! See Biochemistry Sophomore Oscar's attempt at the pipette tip basketball event. We also awarded several awards - most important among them is the Lab Member of the Year Award which goes to Oscar!
      
      
        Lab Olympics
        Student
      
    
  

  
    2024 Nov 02-11
    
    
      Mark goes to Korea as a Visiting Scientist
      Through funding from the Korea Basic Science Institute, Mark was able to spend a week in the institute in Ochang, South Korea with collaborators Donghan Lee (KBSI) and Elias Fernandez (U. Tennessee). This visit also allowed Mark to use one of the world's first 1.2 GHz NMR!
      
      
        Conference
        Student
      
    
  

  
    2024 Oct 28
    
    
      Mark awarded a Dreyfus Lectureship for Undergraduate Institution!
      Thanks to the Camille and Henry Dreyfus Foundation for selecting our application for the Dreyfus Lectureship. This award will support summer research at Georgia Southern, and will also fund a lectureship which we will organize between now and 2027. Watch out for it, we might have something set up for Spring of 2026 or 2027.
      
      
        Grant
      
    
  

  
    2024 Aug 11
    
    
      Grace in another conference - this time, ACS Colorado
      MS student, Grace, presented her work on fluorinated fragment screening to identify new PRL3 inhibitors at the Fall 2024 meeting of the American Chemical Society in Denver, CO. She has now presented several aspects of her undergraduate and graduate research in FIVE different states! Whoop, whoop!
      
      
        Conference
        Student
      
    
  

  
    2024 Aug 01
    
    
      First Grant! We are an NIH-funded lab!
      The National Institutes of Health / National Institute of General Medical Sciences has funded our R16 proposal to study the druggability of oncogenic and pro-metastatic phosphatase, PRL3, and develop novel migrastatics targeting this protein. LET'S GET THINGS DONE!
      
      
        Grant
      
    
  

  
    2024 Jul 28
    
    
      Summer send-off to Athens and Pasadena
      Send off 'party' at Flacos Tacos, Richmond Hill for Davis who is off to pursue his PhD in Biochemistry at the University of Georgia. Thank you to the Rutan family for hosting! Turned out to be a send off 'party' for Victoria as well, who is leaving for college at the California Institute of Technology.

    2024 Jul 01
    
    
      First student-led paper from the lab is available online!
      Our paper, In silico identification of putative druggable pockets in PRL3, a significant oncology target, is now available online. Published at Biochemistry and Biophysics Reports, this work was done by Grace Bennett and Julia Starczewski. This is Grace's first first-author paper, and what I'm sure will be first of many.

Congrats and good luck!

      We took advantage of the proximity of this year's SERMACS in Durham, NC and most of the lab attended and presented.We had a total of 8 posters presenting works of Grace Bennett (Biochem), Ty Spencer (Biochem), Davis Rutan (Biochem), Nick Dillon (Biochem), Jasmine Rodriguez (Biochem), and Alicia Brinegar (Biology).       Collaborations:
      We work closely with faculty from the Department of Biology, and collaborate with researchers from other institutions such as Mercer in Savannah, South, the Georgia Cancer Center, and others.
    
  
  
  
    Interested in Joining?
    
    
      Our lab is affiliated with the Department of Biochemistry, Chemistry, and Physics, and the Department of Biomedical Sciences, and welcome students from our programs to explore research options! 
    

    
      That said, if you are highly passionate about science and research and interested in any of the work we do, or adjacent areas, chat with us to see if there is any opportunity to work together. Any majors at Georgia Southern are welcome to join at various capacities. Majority of the students in the lab are Biomedical Sciences, Biochemistry, and Chemistry majors, but we do not require any prior training or classes. Students can get research credit (BIO, BMED, BCHM, CHEM, or VIP) and/or may be employed as student researchers, depending on funding situation. Summer fellowships are sometimes available from the department or the college.
    
    
    
      We do not typically advertise positions for MS students, as we mostly host students in the accelerated BS-MS Applied Physical Science program. We anticipate trainees from our recently launched PhD in Biomedical Sciences Program. Post-doctoral and staff positions are dependent on funding. Reach out directly if you need a sponsor for a grant or a fellowship. High school and external students may also participate either virtually for computational work or during the summer through research opportunities or transient/dual-enrollment.
    
  




The Science Center at Georgia Southern University’s Armstrong Campus in Savannah, GA, home to the Laboratory of Structural Biology and Drug Discovery.

title: Research in the dC Lab
text:
Our lab mottos, Curiosity leads to cures and The laboratory is our playground reflect our commitment to following our curiosities, not allowing ourselves to be restricted to specific research questions or techniques, but instead continuing to grow to broaden our horizons.

We refer to our group as the Laboratory of Structural Biology and Drug Discovery to reflect our broad interests in the understanding protein structure, function, and dynamics and our mission to develop therapies for various diseases with proteins as primary targets. Beyond this, we are always excited to collaborate with other groups with complementary expertise, where we can leverage our expertise in protein biochemistry and bioNMR.

If any of our projects sound interesting to you, or maybe you need help with anything involving proteins - such as recombinant protein expression or assay development - do not hesitate to reach out. We are always eager to work with similarly passionate folks!





PRL3 Drug Discovery
Our drug discovery program on PRL3, a pro-oncogenic and pro-metastatic phosphatase, leverages an integrated computational, enzyme inhibition, and in vitro screening approach to develop migrastatics and anti-cancer therapies. Different pipelines have resulted to several inhibitors with binding to PRL3 validated by protein- and ligand-observed nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, fluorescence, and isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). We are also designing and optimizing PROTACs and BioPROTACs.

Drug Discovery PTP Drug Screening NIH-funded Cancer Therapy


    






PRL3 Structure and Dynamics
Structures of protein-complexes provide atomic resolution information for the optimization of small molecules and to establish mechanisms of inhibition. Our group uses NMR spectroscopy to characterize the structure of PRL3 bound to small molecule inhibitors. Furthermore, we are interested in the dynamics, at various timescales, associated with PRL3 dynamics, function, and inhibition and in uncovering allosteric networking within PRL3.

Structural Biology PTP Protein Dynamics NIH-funded Molecular Biophysics


  






Druggability of Human PTPs
A number of PTPs are emerging drug targets while several remain understudied and undrugged. We are optimizing the expression and purification of various human PTPs to uncover their structures and begin chemical probe screening. At the same time, we are using established computational tools to evaluate the druggability of PTPs which can accelerate virtual chemical screening pipelines.

Drug Discovery PTP Structural Biology Cancer Therapy


     






Molecular Dynamics of Homeodomains
Homeodomains are small highly conserved structures consisting of three-helix bundles. They are found in transcription factors across genomes, regulating development and cell fate. Several homeodomain structures have been determined and have been used to study DNA-protein interactions. Protein engineering approaches have also resulted to several thermostable homeodomains. We are using molecular dynamics simulations and NMR spectroscopy to study the relationship between structure, function, dynamics, and stability of homeodomains as well as protein allostery.

Structural Biology Homeodomains Protein Dynamics Molecular Biophysics


 






Development of Novel Antibiotics
We extend our interest in human PTPs to bacterial PTPs with a particular focus, currently, on low molecular weight protein tyrosine phosphatases. We use the same drug discovery pipelines we use our human PTP targets and collaborate with microbiologists to evaluate bacterial inhibition of molecules identified. This project is also incorporated in SynZyme, a CURE embedded in our upper-level bioinstrumental course, taught by Dr. dela Cerna and Dr. Landge.

Structural Biology Drug Discovery PTP Antimicrobials CURE


   






Exploratory Drug Screening Efforts
Our lab works on other non-PTP targets, using virtual screening methods, 19F-NMR screening of fluorinated fragment libraries, and nanobody development. These efforts are largely exploratory and early stage and focus on generating hits from virtual and real libraries the lab has access to, as well as molecules synthesized by collaborators within the department, through a drug discovery network. Projects include development of kinase inhibitors, protein-protein interaction inhibitors, and inhibitors of RNA-protein interactions. Trainees involved in this project also engage in assay development and optimization to support these efforts.

Drug Discovery


     






Bacterial Evolution
Lab-directed evolution of microorganisms can be achieved by exposure to different kinds of stressors. These experiments provide insight on evolutionary mechanisms for adaptation and survival, such in involving DNA repair machinery and antibiotic resistance. Growth of bacteria in the presence of other chemical species may also illuminate mechanisms for degradation of these chemical species. This project is a living example of our motto, The laboratory of our playground, with all projects being student-initiated and student-driven.

Microbiology Evolution


  






Membrane Proteins
Membrane proteins, particularly receptors and transporters, are critical components of biological membranes, allowing for communication and material transfer between the interior of cells and their environment. Our lab is interested in GPCRs and membrane protein transporters. Students in Dr. dela Cerna’s Biochemistry 2 Laboratory course participate in several aspects of this project.

title: Laboratory of Structural Biology and Drug Discovery
text:
About Our Research
The lab focuses its investigations on proteins—from the fundamental relationship between structure, function, and dynamics to exploring their potential as molecular targets in various diseases. We work on a variety of protein families with a strong emphasis on protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTPs), a superfamily of phosphatases.
Several drug discovery programs are currently ongoing for development of potential therapeutics, including:

Anti-cancer and anti-metastasis compounds targeting human PTPs
Antimicrobials targeting bacterial PTPs

Additionally, we are interested in uncovering the relationship between protein structure, function, and dynamics. The lab also collaborates with other investigators within and outside Georgia Southern to pursue projects related to biochemistry, broadly.

title: Laboratory of Structural Biology and Drug Discovery
section: What are we currently working on?
text:
What are we currently working on?



Structure and Dynamics
We are currently focused on determining the structure of protein tyrosine phosphatases and their complexes with inhibitors, primarily PRL3 bound to novel inhibitors our group has identified. We are also investigating the relationship of structure, function, and dynamics of homeodomains.





Drug Discovery
Active drug discovery programs in the lab are focused on targeting several PTPs, notably PRL3 for migrastatics and SP-PTP from S. pyogenes for antimicrobial development. We also have active programs against GMPK, MDMX, and ERα.
